records.name: Kyrgyzstan
records.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998 and there is no expression statute, but legal gender recognition has been removed, police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and an active anti-LGBT political campaign is running in the country — in 2023-2024 two discriminatory laws targeted the LGBTI community and restricted LGBTI organisations, with homophobic and transphobic legislator rhetoric accompanying them.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal, a police extortion culture, and the political campaign make being outed risky.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Kyrgyzstan): anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from MPs; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); ECOM data shows high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement.

TGEU Trans Rights Index Map 2024: Kyrgyzstan (2021) joined Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia in removing the right to legal gender recognition; for Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

OutRight International Kyrgyzstan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex activity decriminalised 1998 with age of consent equal at 16; no same-sex marriage or civil unions and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing trans people to change legal gender markers was removed by a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators for Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan) - includes information for trans migrants.
thin: no usable finding

RFE/RL feature on the closure of Bishkek's lone LGBT club (Asanbay car-wash venue): patrons entered furtively through a derelict yard as the atmosphere worsened — documentary evidence of public LGBT life contracting in the capital; no other gay venue remained.

The Guardian (19 Oct 2017): why Bishkek's only gay club closed — the Kyrgyz capital had been a relatively safe haven and liberal beacon in Central Asia until a ban on 'LGBT propaganda'; patrons said 'all of us will be victims at some point', documenting the closing of organised gay nightlife.

records.name: Tajikistan
records.summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.

sources.summary: IPHR report 'Rights for All?' (Feb 2024): consensual same-sex relations decriminalised since 1998, yet authorities introduced a police register of LGBTIQ people in 2016; 2022/2023 police raids brought forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges; ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police documented; the 2022 anti-discrimination law fails to address discrimination — the systematic-risk evidence for a visitor.

Outright International overview (updated Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal throughout the country since independence, no SOGI non-discrimination protection; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion; a 2017 government registry of 'proven' LGBT persons flagged — legality without safety.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services incl. HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing — maps what gender-affirming/HIV care is actually reachable in-country and includes guidance for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): police lure LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database, harvest social-media contacts and extort money (10+ cases in Sughd); forced/sham marriages used against LGBT people with police inaction; the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with UN standards — quantified police-entrapment risk.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): comparative analysis identifying legal barriers and gaps for gay men, MSM and trans people in Tajikistan, built from a questionnaire completed by local partners — documents where the written law protects but practice does not.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 — opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned, and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule — the repressive state context surrounding LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 20, 2013): despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier (1998) there is very little tolerance; those who disclose orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and the community remains one of the most closed in society — social-climate evidence predating the 2016 registry.

records.name: Turkmenistan
records.summary:
Turkmenistan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code not only kept the 'sodomy' provisions but increased both the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them — the current penal-risk read.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues the existence of laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity — official assessment of law plus enforcement climate.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): maps the legal landscape and barriers for LGBT people and PLHIV — deliberately compiled so NGOs, community activists and government can use it when planning advocacy; the standing legal-baseline reference for the country.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

records.name: Syria
records.summary:
Syria is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.

sources.summary: GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025 on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
thin: no usable finding

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

records.name: Bhutan
records.summary:
Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness' (31 Mar 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Erasing 76 Crimes (10 Jun 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point. Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (11 Mar 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 Feb 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (global criminalising-state tally fell 72 to 71). Freshness pass (2026-09-27) confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow': the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page (from c.2014) produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles admins and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira — a first in Bhutanese society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

The Daily Beast (28 Oct 2015): Bhutan's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — 'growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience', no shared language for gay or trans identities, lesbianism under-recognised. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.

records.name: Laos
records.summary: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans in this country, which has a socially visible tradition of trans-feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation — the one-party system restricts all civil society — and no documented recourse. The tourist cities are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque system) more than violent.

sources.summary: thin: no usable finding
thin: no usable finding

Human Dignity Trust history: Laos (with Cambodia) achieved independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system — it has never formally criminalised same-sex conduct, distinguishing it from neighbours that retained colonial sodomy offences.

GlobalGayz first-person account (2000, Richard Ammon): during a week in Vientiane the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the country's LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

Al Jazeera in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential Facebook users ('net idols') face retribution for posts, and 'Proud to be us Laos', the country's only LGBT advocacy group, is quoted; indicates online LGBT expression operates under tightening state attention.

EEAS page (title-verified; body behind JavaScript wall): the EU celebrated International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane — diplomatic visibility for LGBT rights; no further detail retrievable.
